entries.note: The claim concerns OpenAI's interest or intention; public consultation activity cannot establish an absence of private interest.

entries.test: Public recordings and transcripts of Altman's statements before publication would show whether he ever described a real-world ChatGPT use case.
entries.note: The fan-fiction language is rhetorical, but the assertion that he never describes a use case is testable.
The comparison to the least capable human is an insult without a specified domain of performance.
The source explains Altman's messaging through an alleged private motive. What he would like readers to know is not equivalent to what he admits.
The forecast is explicitly framed in terms of likelihood.
There is no shared test for how much of a boom constitutes hot air or how much executives and media created.
Neither the relevant promises nor the media population said to have been fooled is identified.

entries.test: Public evidence of practical benefits from AI deployed between March 2023 and March 2024 would show whether improvements to people's lives were rare or widespread.
entries.note: The plain reading concerns demonstrated practical benefits during the year preceding publication.

entries.test: Company financial disclosures and documented deployments available by publication would show whether companies other than Klarna reported profit improvements attributable to generative AI.
entries.note: “I can find no companies” is qualified by the author's knowledge; the proposition turns it into an unrestricted universal claim.

entries.test: Employment data, documented AI-driven workforce reductions, and operational results from those replacements by March 2024 would test the claim.
entries.note: The proposition removes “does not appear,” making the employment claim firmer.
The source offers a counterfactual about what firms would do if AI had the capability. The proposition substitutes an inferred conclusion for that conditional argument.

entries.test: Public evaluations and reproducible examples from OpenAI models available in March 2024 would show whether hallucinations persisted.
entries.note: “Fix” here means eliminating the problem, rather than merely reducing its frequency.

entries.test: Contemporaneous model evaluations, energy-use measurements, and inference cost and revenue disclosures would show whether practical solutions to these problems were approaching deployment.
entries.note: The claim concerns the state of solutions at publication.

entries.test: Public compute and cost data together with documented consumer adoption and practical uses by March 2024 would test the claimed expense and absence of mass-market applications.
entries.note: Mass-market applications have a plain reading as practical uses adopted by a broad consumer population.

entries.test: Comparable benchmark results and release histories for successive OpenAI models through March 2024 would show whether capability gains over time had slowed.
entries.note: The proposition faithfully extracts the embedded assertion about slowing progress.

entries.test: A publicly available generative AI system independently demonstrated to eliminate hallucinations would falsify the claim.
entries.note: This is a firm, undated claim of permanent inability.
“The future they hyped” does not identify a shared set of deliverables against which proximity can be assessed.
He presents this collapse as a feared possibility, rather than a firm prediction in this passage.

entries.test: An AI investment collapse followed by sector-wide financial performance and venture-capital loss data would show whether the predicted industry-wide harm occurred.
entries.note: The outcome is conditional on an AI bubble bursting, with no deadline.

entries.test: Public demonstrations of substantial capability gains or solutions to core problems using chip and energy technology already available in March 2024 would falsify the asserted technological dependency.
entries.note: The proposition extracts a technological constraint separately from the accompanying allegation about Altman's beliefs. The uncertainty about whether breakthroughs will ever exist does not soften that constraint.

entries.test: Court filings and public legal actions surrounding Sora's public launch would show whether it immediately faced a major legal fight over training data.
entries.note: The training-data inference is hedged, but the launch-related legal prediction is firm. Sora's public launch occurred before the evaluation date.

entries.test: A copyright judgment against an AI company and subsequent documented changes to AI model use across adopting industries would test the predicted sequence.
entries.note: A lawsuit loss alone would not establish the claimed downstream reckoning.
“Possibly necessitating” makes the outcome uncertain. The proposition also strengthens “can't really forget” to an unqualified inability.
The extracted claim combines a present assessment with an explicitly hedged prediction that it will persist.
“Not that much” and “not much more” supply no shared standard for the breadth or significance of capabilities.

entries.test: A publicly demonstrated coherent movie generated by Sora would falsify the prediction.
entries.note: The context distinguishes movies from the short generated clips already discussed.

entries.test: The largest technology companies' reported revenues around the end of 2024 would show whether an AI collapse after roughly three quarters caused severe revenue declines.
entries.note: The forecast's approximately nine-month horizon has passed. “I believe” does not turn a firm prediction into probability language.

entries.test: Following a broad decline in AI usage, public revenue disclosures and data-center utilization reports would show whether big-tech revenue fell and substantial data-center capacity became unused.
entries.note: “Acres of data centers” describes unused capacity, not necessarily many separate facilities.
“I fear” and “could” explicitly frame this as a possible outcome.
